ariel-ob-isaiah-29.partOfSpeech: proper noun (with wordplay on the common noun ʾărîʾēl "altar-hearth")
ariel-ob-isaiah-29.wohChoice: 'Ariel' transliterated at 29:1, 2, 7 (with 'like an Ariel' at v2, the altar-hearth wordplay explained in commentary). ʾôḇ 'a ghost' at 29:4 is governed by ob-yiddeoni-ghosts-familiar-spirits-isaiah (founder ruling 2026-11-26).
ariel-ob-isaiah-29.rationale: ʾărîʾēl is a cipher for Jerusalem ('the city where David encamped'). Ezek 43:15-16 uses the same word for the altar-hearth, and Isa 29:2 plays on that sense: Jerusalem 'shall be to me like an ʾărîʾēl', a place of burning. Because the name and the wordplay depend on keeping one word, the line transliterates with ASV, NRSV and NJPS, and the commentary explains the pun and the alternative derivation 'lion of El' (Wildberger, Isaiah 28-39; Blenkinsopp, AB 19). The ʾôḇ simile of 29:4 ('like that of a ghost from the ground'), formerly governed here, was moved in wave I-3 to ob-yiddeoni-ghosts-familiar-spirits-isaiah (founder ruling 2026-11-26), so that ʾôḇ 'ghost' is governed by one entry at 8:19 and 29:4; the reasons for 'a ghost' against ASV's 'one that hath a familiar spirit' are recorded there. The id is kept unchanged for the stability of existing references.

isa-7-14-virgin-birth-mt-1-22-23-parthen.standardEnglish: Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son (KJV); Behold, the virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son (ASV); Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son (RSV); Look, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son (NRSV)
isa-7-14-virgin-birth-mt-1-22-23-parthen.wohChoice: 'Behold, the virgin shall be with child and shall bear a son' — preserves the LXX *parthenos* 'virgin' which Matthew is explicitly citing; preserves the definite article *hē*, which renders the Hebrew article *hā-* of *hā-ʿalmâ* (the LXX does not add it); the surface English-translation reads the Matthean citation as Matthew presents it (NOT a back-translation to the Hebrew source); the LXX-vs-Hebrew philological dispute is preserved in this glossary apparatus without adjudication; the operational disavowals below explicitly reject (i) Christian-supersessionist 'Jews mistranslated their own scripture' pre-resolution, (ii) Jewish-Christian-polemical 'Christians invented the virgin-birth from a mistranslation' pre-resolution, (iii) Mariological pre-resolution toward immaculate-conception / perpetual-virginity doctrines, (iv) pre-resolution toward the Raëlian canon's reading of the Matthean conception (a child from a woman and one of the creators, TBWTT 4:3).
isa-7-14-virgin-birth-mt-1-22-23-parthen.rationale:
**THE LXX *parthenos* VS HEBREW *ʿalmâ* DISPUTE IS THE LOCUS CLASSICUS OF JEWISH-CHRISTIAN PHILOLOGICAL POLEMIC.** The dispute dates to the 2nd c. CE — Justin Martyr's *Dialogue with Trypho* 71-77 (c. 155-160 CE) preserves the earliest extant Christian-Jewish exchange on the verse: Trypho objects that the LXX is mistranslated and the Hebrew reads 'young woman, not virgin'; Justin defends the LXX rendering and accuses the Jewish scholarly community of corrupting their scriptures. The dispute continues through the medieval and modern periods, with the modern-critical-scholarship consensus position summarized below.

**The Hebrew Isa 7:14 in its 8th-c. BCE setting.** The oracle is delivered to King Ahaz of Judah during the Syro-Ephraimite crisis of 734-732 BCE, when the northern coalition (Rezin of Aram-Damascus + Pekah of Israel) threatened Jerusalem. Isaiah's sign of imminent deliverance: *hinnēh hā-ʿalmâ hārâ wĕ-yōledet bēn wĕ-qārāʾt šĕmô ʿimmānû-ʾēl* 'behold, the young woman is pregnant and shall bear a son and shall call his name Immanuel'. The Hebrew *ʿalmâ* (cognate Ugaritic *ġlmt* in the Krt epic) denotes a young woman of marriageable age — typically pre-marital but emphasizing youth-and-sexual-maturity rather than virginity-per-se. The word that usually carries the sense of virginity is *bĕtûlâ* (Lev 21:13-14; Deut 22:23-29), though not invariably: at Joel 1:8 a *bĕtûlâ* mourns 'the husband of her youth', the usual counter-case to treating *bĕtûlâ* as a technical term for a virgin. The immediate-historical referent of the *ʿalmâ* is debated: (a) the wife of Ahaz (the future mother of Hezekiah — Childs 2001); (b) the wife of Isaiah (cf. Isa 8:3 *hā-nĕbîʾâ* the prophetess); (c) an unnamed young woman known to Ahaz as a sign-figure; (d) a generic Davidic-house figure. The child-Immanuel functions as a SIGN of imminent deliverance: before the child reaches the age of moral discernment, the threatening Syro-Ephraimite coalition will be destroyed (Isa 7:16) — a timeline indicating an 8th-c. BCE near-term referent.

**The LXX *parthenos* rendering.** The Greek LXX (3rd-2nd c. BCE Alexandrian Jewish translation) renders Hebrew *ʿalmâ* with Greek *parthenos*. Greek *parthenos* is itself semantically broader than 'virgin' in classical and Hellenistic usage — it can denote 'unmarried young woman' more generally (cf. LXX Gen 34:3 where Dinah is called *parthenos* AFTER her violation). However, the dominant Hellenistic-Greek lexical sense narrows to 'virgin'. The LXX translator's choice may reflect (a) a faithful rendering of *ʿalmâ* in the broader-sense (young-unmarried-woman); (b) a deliberate-interpretive narrowing toward 'virgin' as part of a developing Jewish messianic-virgin-birth expectation (some 2nd-c. BCE Jewish texts do anticipate virgin-birth motifs — though this is contested); (c) a translator's-error reading *ʿalmâ* as the Hebrew word for virgin. Modern philological consensus (Brown 1993; Levine-Brettler JANT 2017; Childs 2001) treats the LXX rendering as semantically-defensible-within-Greek-range without implying that the LXX translator necessarily intended 'virgin-in-the-strict-sense'.

**The Matthean citation strategy.** Matthew 1:22-23 cites Isa 7:14 LXX as a fulfillment-prophecy of the virgin-conception of Mary. The Matthean citation deploys the LXX *parthenos* in the strict-virgin sense and explicitly identifies Mary as the *parthenos* of Isa 7:14. This is one of Matthew's signature *hina plērōthē* fulfillment-formulae (cf. Mt 1:22; 2:15; 2:17-18; 2:23; 4:14-16; 8:17; 12:17-21; 13:14-15; 13:35; 21:4-5; 27:9-10) — a Matthean structural-theological device that frames the entire Gospel as the eschatological-fulfillment of Israel's scriptures. The Matthean theological move (Davies-Allison ICC 1.209-217; Brown 1993 145-150) is the appropriation of the Isaianic-sign for the Mary-conception narrative — a 1st-c. Christian theological-interpretation of a 8th-c. Hebrew text.

**The Jewish-critical reading.** Modern Jewish scholarly tradition (Levine-Brettler JANT 2017 ad loc.; the older traditional Jewish reading from Rashi onward) treats the LXX *parthenos* as a Christian-apologetic appropriation of an oracle whose Hebrew sense is 'young woman' and whose 8th-c. BCE referent is the imminent-deliverance Syro-Ephraimite-crisis sign. The Jewish-critical reading does NOT accept the Matthean appropriation as the Hebrew text's primary meaning; it preserves the Isa 7:14 oracle in its historical-Israelite context as a sign-oracle to Ahaz.

**The Brown 1993 comprehensive treatment.** R. E. Brown, *The Birth of the Messiah*, 2nd ed. (Anchor Bible Reference Library 1993), the comprehensive scholarly monograph on the birth-narratives, treats the Isa 7:14 / Mt 1:22-23 dispute systematically. Brown's position: (a) the Hebrew *ʿalmâ* does NOT specifically mean 'virgin'; (b) the LXX *parthenos* is a defensible-Greek rendering that does NOT necessarily-imply the strict-virgin sense; (c) Matthew's appropriation is a 1st-c. Christian theological-reading that builds on the LXX rendering; (d) the historical question 'did Mary conceive virginally' is theological-not-philological and is left unresolved by the philological analysis. Brown's treatment is the modern critical-scholarship benchmark.

**Cross-corpus reach.** The Isa 7:14 fulfillment-citation is paired in Matthew with the Isa 8:8, 10 *ʿimmānû-ʾēl* attestations and the broader Matthean Emmanuel-frame-inclusio (Mt 1:23 ↔ Mt 28:20 — see `emmanuel-frame-inclusio-mt-1-23-mt-28-20-divine-presence-cross-corpus-kupp`). The virgin-conception narrative cross-corpus to: Lk 1:26-38 (the Lukan annunciation-narrative with *parthenos* at Lk 1:27); the apocryphal Protoevangelium of James (2nd c. CE) developing the perpetual-virginity tradition; the Qur'an's parallel virgin-conception narrative at Sura 19 (Maryam) and Sura 3:42-47 (the Annunciation to Maryam).

**Named scholarship.** R. E. Brown, *The Birth of the Messiah*, 2nd ed. (Anchor Bible Reference Library 1993), the comprehensive monograph; W. D. Davies and D. C. Allison, *A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Gospel According to Saint Matthew*, vol. 1 (ICC, T&T Clark 1988) 209-217; U. Luz, *Matthew 1-7* (Hermeneia, Fortress 2007) 95-100; R. T. France, *The Gospel of Matthew* (NICNT, Eerdmans 2007) 56-58; D. A. Hagner, *Matthew 1-13* (WBC 33A, Word 1993) 19-22; B. S. Childs, *Isaiah* (OTL, Westminster John Knox 2001) on Isa 7:14; J. D. W. Watts, *Isaiah 1-33*, 2nd ed. (WBC 24, Nelson 2005) on Isa 7:14; M. A. Sweeney, *Isaiah 1-39* (FOTL 16, Eerdmans 1996) on Isa 7:14; H. Wildberger, *Isaiah 1-12* (CC, Fortress 1991) on Isa 7:14; A.-J. Levine and M. Z. Brettler, eds., *The Jewish Annotated New Testament*, 2nd ed. (Oxford 2017) ad loc.; A. J. Saldarini, 'Matthew', in *The Jewish Annotated New Testament* (Oxford 2017); J. Schaberg, *The Illegitimacy of Jesus*, expanded ed. (Sheffield Phoenix 2006), the historical-critical-feminist treatment.

Bidirectional cross-references with existing Hebrew central entries `elohim-as-translation`.

**Lens-discipline operational disavowals.** (i) **No Christian-supersessionist 'Jews mistranslated their own scripture' pre-resolution.** The patristic / Reformation-era / modern-Christian-apologetic reading that accuses Jewish scholars of corrupting the Isa 7:14 text or 'misunderstanding their own scripture' is a downstream Christian-anti-Judaic move that the WoH-Translation does NOT endorse. The LXX is a Jewish translation; the Hebrew is the Jewish source; the philological dispute is about the Hebrew sense of *ʿalmâ* and the LXX-Greek rendering, not about Jewish-scholarly-bad-faith. (ii) **No Jewish-Christian-polemical 'Christians invented the virgin-birth from a mistranslation' pre-resolution.** The reverse-polemical move — that the entire virgin-birth narrative is a Christian-apologetic invention built on a LXX-mistranslation — also pre-resolves a complex theological-historical question that the philological data does not by itself decide. The WoH-Translation preserves the philological dispute without adjudication. (iii) **No Mariological pre-resolution.** The Catholic-Orthodox doctrinal developments of immaculate-conception (Pius IX 1854) and perpetual-virginity tradition are downstream Christian-theological developments that the WoH-Translation does NOT pre-resolve onto the 1st-c. text. (iv) **No Raëlian-canon pre-resolution.** The Raëlian canon reads the Matthean conception as the birth of a child from a woman and one of the creators: the creators 'decide to bring forth a child issued from a woman and from one of their own' (TBWTT 4:3, citing Matt 1:18, 20). The canon does not speak of preserved genetic material of Mary and does not cite Isa 7:14. Its passage on a preserved cell (ETTMTTP 2:62, Jesus 'whom we were able to recreate from a cell we had preserved before his crucifixion') concerns the recreation of Jesus after his death, not his conception. **This entry acknowledges-without-endorsement the Raëlian-canon citation** per the established cross-corpus precedents; the WoH-Translation does NOT adopt the Raëlian framing on the surface. (v) **Preserve the dispute, do not adjudicate.** The LXX *parthenos* / Hebrew *ʿalmâ* dispute is preserved as a documented philological-Jewish-Christian dispute; the WoH-Translation reproduces the Matthean LXX-citation on the surface (Matthew is the cited authority, and Matthew cites the LXX) and documents the underlying Hebrew dispute in this apparatus.
